newsitem.title: UK: Nationalists call for probe in N.Irish killing.
newsitem.headline: Nationalists call for probe in N.Irish killing.

text.p: Nationalist leaders in Northern Ireland on Friday demanded a British inquiry into why police failed to stop the savage, fatal beating of a Roman Catholic man by a Protestant mob.

Gerry Adams, leader of the IRA's politican wing Sinn Fein, challenged Britain's new Northern Ireland Secretary Mo Mowlam to investigate the killing in the bitterly divided town of Portadown, 25 miles (40 km) south of Belfast.

"What I am calling for is for Mo Mowlam to authorise an inquiry into that incident and I am calling for the RUC officers involved to be suspended from duty pending the outcome of that inquiry," Adams told BBC radio. The RUC, or Royal Ulster Constabulary, is Northern Ireland's police force.
Police sources said their officers were outnumbered by pro-British "Loyalist" thugs who isolated two Catholic nationalist men early on April 27 in Portadown and beat them.
Robert Hamill, 25, a father of two, never regained consciousness and died on Thursday night in a Belfast hospital.

Police said they have already questioned some people about the attack. "This was a brutal sectarian attack and my officers will be unrelenting in their search for the culprits," said Portadown police commander Freddie Hall.
The incident was the latest in a spate of sectarian attacks in Northern Ireland, where guerrillas of the Irish Republican Army are fighting for an end to British rule.
Politicians hope the election of a new Labour government in Britain last week may kick-start the stalled peace process.
Sinn Fein chief negotiator Martin McGuinness told the BBC that Irish people expected Labour to apply "new thinking, new language, new imagination to the search for peace" in the British province.
The Irish News, Belfast's nationalist newspaper, quoted an unnamed eyewitness as saying Hamill had been "danced on" and called a "Fenian (Catholic) bastard" by hoodlums in a 30-strong gang.

Police sources said officers were dispersing a dozen loyalists, who back British rule of Northern Ireland, when a coachload of drunken louts arrived and laid into four "totally innocent" Catholics who had just emerged from a dance hall.
"Police found themselves totally outnumbered until they could get (extra police) assistance," a security source said.
Hamill was the second Catholic man to be killed in a year in Portadown, where sectarian tension runs high between pro-British Protestants and Catholics who want a united Ireland.
Policing is one of Northern Ireland's most contentious issues. RUC chiefs deny Catholic charges that the largely Protestant-officered Royal Ulster Constabulary is biased.
Britain says Sinn Fein will be given a seat at talks to thrash out all controversial issues if IRA guerrillas abandon their fight against British rule.
